svg.title: The six components of a tool description, and one description that has all six
svg.desc: A hand-drawn figure in two columns. The left column numbers the six things every tool description carries: a verb-object name with no adjectives or clashing prefixes; a ten-to-fifteen-word summary, which is what decides whether the model reaches for the tool; one sentence on when to use it; one sentence on when not to, naming the tool to use instead, because negative guidance prevents most miscalls; parameters with type, optionality, default, and one line each, using enums wherever a free string would do; and one worked example with input and expected output. The right column shows a single search_orders description with all six parts present and numbered to match. Captions warn against a three-hundred-token description that is mostly disclaimers, noting disclaimers belong in code because the tool can refuse invalid input, and that the description should make the tool easy to call right rather than hard to call wrong.
svg.text: Six things every tool description carries
Treat it like a docstring an unfamiliar contractor will read exactly once, just before calling it.
What it does, in ten to fifteen words. This is what
decides whether to reach for it.
One sentence naming the tool to use instead.
Type, required or optional, default, one line each.
Enums wherever a free string would do.
Input and expected output. Examples beat paragraphs
One description that carries all six
summary: Look up an order by id or by
use when: the user supplies an order id
do not use: for refunds. Use issue_refund.
order_id string optional the order id
Anti-pattern: a 300-token description that is mostly disclaimers and edge-case caveats.
Disclaimers belong in code — the tool can refuse an invalid input. The description makes the tool easy to call right, not hard to call wrong.
